title: How Flamethrowers Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how flamethrowers work, tracing their history from an ancient Greek/Byzantine tube-and-pump design using Greek fire, through the Chinese double-action bellows, the early 1900s German design by Richard Fiedler, the three-tank handheld model, the 1942 napalm improvement, and their use on boats, tanks, and in forest firefighting. They also cover a South African car theft deterrent that shot fire at intruders, mention fire breathers, and close with plugs for live shows, Kiva lending, and a listener mail about altering hotel art.

segments.title: Opening banter and George Carlin bit
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the holiday weekend and George Carlin's joke about why flamethrowers exist, then mention modern weapons like flechette bombs.

segments.title: Ancient flamethrowers and Greek fire
segments.summary: The hosts describe an early crude flamethrower from the fifth century BC that shot hot coal and sulfur through a tube, then discuss Greek fire, a petroleum and sulfur mixture used by the Byzantines in naval battles and on the walls of Constantinople.

segments.title: Pumps, bellows, and the decline after gunpowder
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck compare the Byzantine single-action bellows pump with the Chinese double-action bellows that gave a continuous stream, then note that flamethrowers faded for about a thousand years after gunpowder arrived.

segments.title: German revival and the three-tank design
segments.summary: The Germans revived the flamethrower before World War One, credited to engineer Richard Fiedler in 1901. The hosts explain the handheld three-tank design: two outer tanks of fuel, a central tank of compressed butane that pressurizes the fuel and serves as the pilot flame.

segments.title: Ignition and fuel release mechanics
segments.summary: The hosts walk through how the igniter works: a battery-driven spark lights the butane pilot flame, and pulling the fuel release trigger pulls back a valve plug so fuel rushes to the nozzle and ignites.

segments.title: Napalm, boats, and the Zippo flamethrower
segments.summary: In 1942 the Army Chemical Warfare Service developed napalm, a thickened gasoline that carries farther and sticks to targets. It was mounted on PT boats, and early ignition failures earned the nickname Zippo flamethrowers. The hosts describe a two-man team and tactics of cover fire before a flamethrower operator approaches a cave.

segments.title: Tanks, range, firefighting, and South African car deterrent
segments.summary: Flamethrowers were also mounted on tanks, with a backpack range of about fifty yards. Forest firefighters use them for prescribed burns. The hosts describe a South African car theft deterrent called the Blaster that shot gas flames from the car's doors, and briefly mention fire breathers.

segments.title: Live show plugs, Kiva, and listener mail
segments.summary: Plugs for upcoming New York live shows and the Kiva micro-lending team, then a listener named Guy describes altering hotel art. The hosts sign off with a closing ad.
